extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, public administration scholars, and policymakers interested in criteria for good government
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the standards and evaluative criteria the author gives for judging the quality and fitness of political institutions and administrations across different stages of social development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to make itself obeyed (enforcement/Order)
rubrics_metrics.description: Government must be able to make its ordinances obeyed; those who cannot enforce obedience cannot be said to govern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as an indispensable attribute and a necessary condition: a government must secure submission to public authority (cessation of private violence). Example/anti-pattern: a polity that cannot enforce its laws does not govern. But the author warns this capacity is not the ultimate end of government—merely requisite to achieve higher purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduciveness to Progress (primary criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The best government is that which is most conducive to Progress—understood as the increase of social good (and including preservation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author argues Progress includes Order; therefore, overall excellence of government is judged by how it furthers improvement in wealth, virtue, intelligence, and activity. Guidance: prefer the government that promotes net gain in social good rather than merely preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of existing goods (Order/Permanence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Order means preservation of all kinds and amounts of good which already exist (cessation of private violence, security).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although necessary (and often classed separately), preservation is presented as part of Progress rather than an independent ultimate aim. Examples: police maintaining personal and property security; maintaining stability so improvements are not squandered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion of virtue, intelligence, and practical activity in the people
rubrics_metrics.description: A primary element of good government is its tendency to foster moral, intellectual, and active qualities among the governed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is framed as a form of national education: governments should increase the sum of desirable qualities (industry, integrity, justice, prudence, enterprise, courage, originality) because these qualities are both ends and the means by which government can be effective. Anti-patterns: institutions that demoralize or leave the populace ignorant and selfish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and fitness of governmental machinery (administrative arrangements)
rubrics_metrics.description: The merit of institutions includes the degree to which they organize and apply the moral/intellectual worth of citizens to public affairs—i.e., the design of machinery for government action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete elements listed: proper tests for qualifications of officers, fair promotion rules, appropriate distribution of business, methodical order of transaction, intelligible records, clear allocation of responsibilities, and checks against negligence/favoritism/jobbery. The machinery is the means by which popular virtue and intelligence are brought to bear; a good apparatus increases effectiveness even when human virtue is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity, freedom of discussion, and press as enabling checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicity and liberty of discussion are essential to allow observation, criticism, and control of public officials and administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without publicity the public cannot check or encourage officials. The text emphasizes publicity's role in rendering other checks effective: it facilitates scrutiny, debate, and censure which improve administration; if the public is indifferent, however, publicity alone will not produce good outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration of justice (procedural design and accessibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial efficacy depends on both the moral quality of actors and the procedural machinery: rules of evidence, procedure, access, and methods for eliciting truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: forms of procedure adapted to elicit truth, ease of access to tribunals, arrangements for detecting crimes and apprehending offenders. Anti-patterns: judges and witnesses corrupt or lying; procedures ill-adapted to truth-seeking, which render even well-designed institutions ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security of person and property (crime repression as basis for progress)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective repression of crime and reliable security for person and property are prerequisites for both Order and Progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: effective policing not only preserves order but fosters production, social trust, and moral sentiments conducive to improvement. Lack of security deters productive effort and undermines public spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound finance and taxation (economy and just distribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: A just and economical financial system that does not unduly burden industry is essential for preserving and increasing national wealth and for educating moral sentiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific guidance: economy preserves existing wealth and encourages creation of more; fair burden distribution sets examples of morality and good conscience; taxation should avoid impeding industry or unnecessary interference with liberty. Anti-patterns: bad finance that impoverishes or demoralizes the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentive alignment and accountability of officials
rubrics_metrics.description: Government is best when the interest of the functionary coincides with his duty and when there are apt checks to make individuals known and responsible for their acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideal: officials’ private interests align with public duties; systems should foster clear responsibility and known accountability. Practical guidance: selection tests, promotion rules, records, and checks to prevent negligence and favoritism. Caveat: no system acts without some virtuous agents and an attentive public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding corruption and fostering public engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions should prevent bribery, corruption, venality, and apathy among electors and officials; public vigilance is necessary to make machinery effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/anti-patterns: electors choosing candidates for money rather than merit; judges taking bribes; officials appointed who have private interests in office outcomes. Even the best apparatus fails if the public is too ignorant, passive, or careless to exercise oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition and balance of personnel (diversity of temperaments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Political bodies should include persons of both cautious and bold temperaments (old and young, established and ambitious) so tendencies temper one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: natural admixture generally suffices if not disturbed by artificial regulation; ensuring no extreme dominance of one character-type helps prevent wandering into excesses—e.g., excessive caution or reckless innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of form of government to the society's stage of development
rubrics_metrics.description: The most appropriate polity depends on a people's current state of cultivation; institutions that are fit for one stage may be disastrously unfit for another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in very uncivilized societies a nearly despotic government that makes itself obeyed may be necessary to teach obedience and industry; 'leading-strings' paternal despotism may be appropriate to train people toward self-government. Conversely, institutions that helped achieve a stage (e.g., Egyptian hierarchy, Chinese paternal despotism) can later block further progress if they inhibit mental liberty and individuality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize harm to existing goods while pursuing improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: In seeking required improvements, a government must avoid doing damage to what is already possessed or valuable; Progress should not destroy permanence unnecessarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle: do not pursue a gain in one respect at more than equivalent loss in another. Example: teaching obedience to savages must not convert them into permanent slaves. Institutions appropriate for one transitional stage should be temporary and not entrench handicaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government as organizer of available public virtue (organizing, not creating, human worth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Government’s role is partly to organize the existing moral/intellectual/active worth in the people to conduct collective affairs effectively; much of government quality lies in how it harnesses what exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinction: what government makes of the citizens (educative role) vs. what it does with them (administrative action). Good constitutions bring the general standard of intelligence and honesty and the best individuals more directly to bear on government tasks.
